walkthrough:
**What we have**

We have 150 patients taking the drug. We want to test whether their mean protein concentration is **less than** 0.185. We are given $n = 150$, $\sum x = 27.0$ and $\sum x^2 = 5.01$. We have no value for the population variance, so we will estimate it from the sample.

**Sample mean (earns B1)**

$\bar{x}$ ("x-bar") means the mean of the sample: add up all the $x$ values and divide by how many there are.

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n} = \frac{27.0}{150} = 0.18$$

**Unbiased estimate of the variance (earns M1)**

Because we only have a sample, we use the "unbiased estimate" of the population variance, which divides by $n - 1$ (not $n$). The formula is

$$s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum x^2 - \frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}\right)$$

Build it in pieces. $27.0^2 = 729$, and $\dfrac{729}{150} = 4.86$. So $5.01 - 4.86 = 0.15$. Then divide by $n - 1 = 149$:

$$s^2 = \frac{0.15}{149} = 0.0010067$$

$$s = \sqrt{0.0010067} = 0.031729$$

(The mark scheme finds the same thing by $\sqrt{\frac{150}{149}} \times \sqrt{\frac{5.01}{150} - 0.18^2}$.)

**Hypotheses (earns B1)**

Let $\mu$ be the population mean concentration of the protein for patients taking the drug.

$$\text{H}_0: \mu = 0.185$$

$$\text{H}_1: \mu < 0.185$$

$\text{H}_0$ says the drug makes no difference. $\text{H}_1$ is one-tailed ("less than") because the researcher wants to know if the drug lowers the concentration.

**Distribution under $\text{H}_0$**

The sample is large ($n = 150$), so by the central limit theorem the sample mean $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal, even though we do not know how single readings are distributed. Under $\text{H}_0$ its mean is $0.185$ and its standard deviation (the "standard error") is $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{150}}$.

**Test statistic: set up (earns M1)**

$$z = \frac{\bar{x} - 0.185}{\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{150}}} = \frac{0.18 - 0.185}{\dfrac{0.031729}{\sqrt{150}}}$$

The divisor must contain $\sqrt{150}$ because we are dealing with a mean of 150 readings.

**Test statistic: calculate (earns A1)**

Top: $0.18 - 0.185 = -0.005$.

Bottom: $\sqrt{150} = 12.2474$, and $\dfrac{0.031729}{12.2474} = 0.0025906$.

$$z = \frac{-0.005}{0.0025906} = -1.930$$

Keep the negative sign: the sample mean is below 0.185.

**Compare (earns M1)**

For a 1% one-tailed test, in the lower tail, the critical value is the $z$ with $\Phi(z) = 0.01$. By symmetry this is minus the value with $\Phi = 0.99$, so $z_{\text{crit}} = -2.326$ (percentage points table).

The rule: reject $\text{H}_0$ only if $z$ is **less than** (further left than) $-2.326$. We have

$$-1.930 > -2.326$$

so our $z$ is not in the rejection region. (The same conclusion follows from probabilities: $\Phi(-1.930) = 0.0268 > 0.01$.) Quick check: both numbers are negative; $-1.93$ is closer to 0, so it is the bigger number.

**Conclusion in context (earns A1 FT)**

We do not reject $\text{H}_0$. In words: there is no evidence, at the 1% significance level, that the mean concentration of the protein in patients taking the drug is less than for patients not taking the drug.

**Final answer**

$z = -1.930$ is not less than $-2.326$, so do not reject $\text{H}_0$: there is no evidence (at the 1% level) that the concentration with the drug is less than without it.

hints: A Type II error means not rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is actually false. First find the boundary of the acceptance region for $\bar{x}$: set $\dfrac{c - 0.185}{s/\sqrt{150}}$ equal to the critical $z$-value for the test (lower tail, 1%).
Rearrange that equation to get the critical value $c$ of the sample mean. $\text{H}_0$ is accepted when $\bar{x}$ is bigger than $c$.
Now suppose the true mean is 0.175: $\bar{X}$ is normal with mean 0.175 and the same standard error $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{150}}$. Standardise $c$ using $0.175$ in place of $0.185$.
A Type II error happens when $\bar{x} > c$ under the true mean, which is an upper tail: write $1 - \Phi(\cdot)$ of your new $z$.
Evaluate $1 - \Phi(\cdot)$ with a table or your calculator's normal cdf and round to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
**What a Type II error is**

A Type II error is accepting (not rejecting) $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is really false. Here the true mean is 0.175, so $\text{H}_0$ ($\mu = 0.185$) is false. A Type II error happens if the sample mean is high enough that the test fails to reject $\text{H}_0$. So first we need to know exactly which sample means lead to "not reject".

**Find the critical value of the sample mean (earns M1)**

The test rejects $\text{H}_0$ when $z$ is below $-2.326$. For the cut-off sample mean $c$:

$$\frac{c - 0.185}{\dfrac{0.031729}{\sqrt{150}}} = -2.326$$

The standard error is $\dfrac{0.031729}{\sqrt{150}} = 0.0025906$ (as in part (i)). The mark scheme needs 0.185 (the mean under $\text{H}_0$) and $\sqrt{150}$ here.

**Solve for $c$ (earns A1)**

Multiply both sides by $0.0025906$: $-2.326 \times 0.0025906 = -0.006026$. Then add $0.185$:

$$c = 0.185 - 0.006026 = 0.17897$$

So we reject $\text{H}_0$ if $\bar{x} < 0.179$ and do not reject it if $\bar{x} > 0.179$. (Notice that in part (i) the sample mean 0.18 is just above this boundary, which agrees with the answer there.)

**Standardise using the true mean (earns M1)**

Now the sample mean has its real distribution: $\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(0.175, \left(\dfrac{0.031729}{\sqrt{150}}\right)^2\right)$. Convert the boundary $0.17897$ to a $z$ value with the **true** mean $0.175$:

$$z = \frac{0.17897 - 0.175}{0.0025906} = \frac{0.00397}{0.0025906} = 1.534$$

(Using the unrounded boundary, $0.178973$, gives $1.5337$, which is also $1.534$.)

**Find the probability (earns M1)**

A Type II error means $\bar{X} > 0.17897$, the area to the right of $z = 1.534$. The calculator and tables give areas to the left, so

$$\text{P}(\text{Type II error}) = \text{P}(Z > 1.534) = 1 - \Phi(1.534)$$

**Calculate (earns A1)**

$\Phi(1.534) = 0.9375$ (normal table or calculator).

$$1 - 0.9375 = 0.0625$$

Rounded to 3 significant figures, $0.0625$ (answers from $0.0610$ to $0.0628$ are accepted). Quick check: the true mean is only a little below the boundary, so a fairly small chance of a wrong "accept" is sensible.
